summary:
SPACE VAULT: Escape from Earth is a 2D pixel-art adventure game inspired by classic Pokémon-style RPGs. Players control Joe Peng, an alien spy trapped on Earth who must explore laboratories, collect spacecraft components, defeat four Scientists and build a spaceship to escape.

The game combines exploration, turn-based battles and spacecraft engineering challenges. Each Scientist introduces different obstacles involving power management, spacecraft mass, communication systems and mission readiness. Players must select suitable components, manage limited resources and overcome engineering challenges to progress.

Developed using Godot, SPACE VAULT draws on NASA CubeSat resources and NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions materials to guide its spacecraft design and mission-planning concepts. It also uses numerical data from the NASA Earth Fact Sheet, including Earth's surface gravity, for launch calculations.

SPACE VAULT aims to make space mission design fun, accessible and educational by allowing players to experiment with engineering decisions and understand how spacecraft systems work together to achieve a successful mission.
details:
Space Vault: Escape From Earth is a 2D top-down pixel-art space exploration and systems-engineering RPG. Inspired by classic titles like Pokémon and Stardew Valley, the game combines narrative exploration, turn-based tactical battles, and real-world aerospace engineering constraints into an interactive escape mission.

What It Does & How It Works

Players control Joe Peng, a protagonist attempting to escape Earth after scientists intercept and dismantle his spacecraft, accompanied by his flying companion Matcha. The gameplay loop flows through three interconnected stages:

Exploration & Lab Infiltration: Players navigate top-down 2D pixel-art environments—triggering interactive spots, discovering Matcha, and infiltrating the laboratory facility to reclaim stripped spacecraft hardware.

Turn-Based Engineering Boss Battles: Outside the laboratory, four lead scientists (Dr. Niq, Dr. Gabby, Dr. Ahmed, and Dr. Celine) block Joe's path to the launch pad. Instead of traditional combat, each boss initiates a specialized aerospace engineering simulation test:

Dr. Niq (Solar Eclipse Shadow): Tests battery endurance during a 35-minute orbital eclipse without solar generation.

Dr. Gabby (Gravity Well Crush): Tests rocket thrust and launch feasibility under extra payload mass.

Dr. Ahmed (Signal Jammer): Tests science data transmission within a restricted ground-contact window.

Dr. Celine (Escape Velocity Crisis): Combines power, launch mass, and communications checks simultaneously.

During battles, players use Inspect to diagnose system readiness, engage tactical Countermeasures (such as power-saving mode or payload jettisoning), and run Simulations to deal damage when their spacecraft passes the engineering threshold.

Spacecraft Workbench Assembly: Defeating each scientist unlocks higher-tier rocket components across six core subsystems (Engine, Battery, Solar Panel, Science Scanner, Communication Module, and Fuel Tank). Players open the Ship Builder Workbench between encounters to balance mass, power consumption, and component specs before challenging the next scientist and launching off Earth.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Gamified Aerospace & Systems Engineering Education: Rather than presenting space mission design as dry formulas, the game translates real NASA systems engineering concepts—power budgets, eclipse survival, payload mass limits, and downlink bandwidth—into intuitive, hands-on problem-solving.

Iterative Critical Thinking: Because failed simulations penalize the player and require returning to the workbench to rebalance trade-offs, players learn how changing one subsystem (e.g., adding a heavier battery or scanner) impacts launch mass and power draw across the entire spacecraft.

Accessible STEM Engagement: Wrapping technical mission-readiness checks in a familiar retro RPG aesthetic lowers the barrier to entry for students and casual players curious about how spacecraft are engineered.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

Game Engine & Frameworks: Godot Engine 4 (with the Dialogue Manager plugin for branching narrative sequences and custom UI/tween systems).

Programming Languages: GDScript (for player movement, scene transitions, state persistence, battle mechanics, and physics-based engineering simulations).

Art & Animation: Aseprite (for creating custom 2D pixel-art characters, multi-directional sprite sheets, and animated battle encounters) alongside pixel-art tilesets sourced from itch.io for environment level design.

Development Environment & Collaboration: Git, and GitHub for distributed team version control, alongside Windows development hardware powered by an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti GPU and 24 GB RAM.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

Engineering Trade-Offs Over Simple Currency: Instead of relying on standard RPG gold or linear stat upgrades, our team designed a constraint-driven progression system where every part has realistic mass, power, and data trade-offs—forcing players to engineer a balanced spacecraft rather than simply equipping the most expensive items.

Cohesive Visual & Narrative Direction: We paired custom pixel-art environments and expressive character animations (including speaker-focus highlights and Matcha's dry, analytical commentary) with structured UI layouts so technical telemetry—like battery watt-hours, payload mass, and megabytes transmitted—remains readable at a 640×360 retro resolution.

Modular Team Architecture: Splitting development between narrative exploration scenes and a self-contained battle/workbench state machine allowed our team to build, test, and integrate individual encounters cleanly while preserving player progression across scenes.
